oneLine: Open models caught up with closed ones, so serving models well stopped being a frontier-lab niche and became a skill every serious AI product team needs.
summary:
In late 2022 the people doing this work numbered in the hundreds, mostly inside a few labs, and it looked like everyone else would rent intelligence through an API forever. That future didn't arrive. Training stayed hard but not impossibly so, and millions of open models now sit on Hugging Face, with the strongest ones trailing the best closed models by weeks rather than years.

Once a team can run the weights itself, three things become engineering choices instead of a vendor's defaults: how fast responses arrive, how often the service is up, and what each token costs. The Preface argues that this is why an inference strategy now separates differentiated products from thin wrappers, and why the field rewards newcomers: it is young, the problems run from kernels to clusters, and the experts are still few.

mechanism.title: Labs held the weights
mechanism.body: In 2022 only a few companies trained frontier models; everyone else called their APIs.

mechanism.title: Open models caught up
mechanism.body: From late 2024, open releases matched closed models within weeks or months on capability.

mechanism.title: Weights mean control
mechanism.body: Running your own model turns latency, availability and cost into things you can engineer.

mechanism.title: Strategy becomes mandatory
mechanism.body: Competitive AI products now need people who can serve models fast, cheaply and reliably.

callout.name: You are early
callout.body: The demand for inference skills is far larger than the number of people who have them. A field this young lets a newcomer reach the frontier quickly, because most of the hard problems are still open.

figureRefs.lookFor: How steeply the count of public models has climbed in five years.
Open and closed models each crossing the same capability lines, a little apart in time.
Customisation adding capability while you keep control of latency, reliability and cost.

keyCards.label: Latency
keyCards.title: Tune for real time
keyCards.body: Shared APIs optimise for throughput across customers; your own deployment can optimise for one fast user.

keyCards.label: Availability
keyCards.title: From two nines to four
keyCards.body: Dedicated deployments can reach 99.99% uptime, where shared APIs often sit near 99%.

keyCards.label: Cost
keyCards.title: Large savings at scale
keyCards.body: At high volume an open model can cost a fraction of a closed API per token.

workedExample.title: What a nine of availability buys you
workedExample.setup: Availability targets sound close together, but each extra nine cuts allowed downtime by ten. Take a 30-day month: 30 × 24 × 60 = 43,200 minutes. The allowed downtime is that total multiplied by the fraction of time the service may be down.

conclusion.text: Moving from two nines to four nines takes a month's outages from most of a working day to a few minutes. That difference is why some teams move to dedicated deployments.

checkQuestion.prompt: A dedicated deployment promises four nines (99.99%) of availability. How many minutes of downtime does that allow in a 30-day month?
checkQuestion.methodHint: Count the minutes in the month, then multiply by the fraction of time the service may be down.
checkQuestion.explanation: Four nines leaves 0.01% of the month for outages: about four minutes. The tempting slip is to use 1% (two nines), which gives 432 minutes, a hundred times more.
checkQuestion.sourceQuote: possible to achieve four nines or better with dedicated deployments of open models

reflect.prompt: Explain to a product manager why switching from a closed-model API to an open model you deploy yourself changes what your team can promise users. Name the three dimensions the Preface highlights.
reflect.modelAnswer: With a closed API, latency, uptime and price are whatever the vendor offers, and the vendor tunes them for all of its customers at once. When we run an open model ourselves, those become engineering decisions. We can tune the deployment for low latency on our own traffic instead of the vendor's throughput-first setup. We can run redundant dedicated capacity and aim for four nines rather than living with an API's outages. And at our volume we can pay far less per token, because we choose the hardware, the batching and the model size. The trade is that we now own the serving work, which is exactly what inference engineering is.
points: Latency: a dedicated deployment can be tuned for real-time use rather than shared throughput.
Availability: dedicated deployments can reach four nines instead of an API's two.
Cost: at scale, open models can be dramatically cheaper per token.
The price of control is owning the serving work yourself.
